# Introduction#

# Overview#

CuTe DSL is a Python-based domain-specific language (DSL) designed for dynamic compilation of
high-performance GPU kernels.  It evolved from the C++ CUTLASS library and is
now available as a decorator-based DSL.

Its primary goals are:

- 
Zero-cost abstraction, DSL is a zero-cost abstraction thanks to Hybrid DSL approach.

- 
Consistent with CuTe C++, allowing users to express GPU kernels with full
control of the hardware.

- 
JIT compilation for both host and GPU execution.

- 
DLPack integration, enabling seamless
interop with frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, JAX).

- 
JIT caching, so that repeated calls to the same function benefit from
cached IR modules.

- 
Native types and type inference to reduce boilerplate and improve
performance.

- 
Optional lower-level control, offering direct access to GPU backends or
specialized IR dialects.

# Decorators#

CuTe DSL provides two main Python decorators for generating optimized code via dynamic compilation:

- 
@jit — Host-side JIT-compiled functions

- 
@kernel — GPU kernel functions

Both decorators can optionally use a preprocessor that automatically expands Python control flow (loops, conditionals) into operations consumable by the underlying IR.

# @jit#

Declares JIT-compiled functions that can be invoked from Python or from other CuTe DSL functions.

Decorator Parameters:

- 
preprocessor:

- 
True (default) — Automatically translate Python flow control (e.g., loops, if-statements) into IR operations.

- 
False — No automatic expansion; Python flow control must be handled manually or avoided.

Call-site Parameters:

- 
no_cache:

- 
True — Disables JIT caching, forcing a fresh compilation each call.

- 
False (default) — Enables caching for faster subsequent calls.

# @kernel#

Defines GPU kernel functions, compiled as specialized GPU symbols through dynamic compilation.

Decorator Parameters:

- 
preprocessor:

- 
True (default) — Automatically expands Python loops/ifs into GPU-compatible IR operations.

- 
False — Expects manual or simplified kernel implementations.

Kernel Launch Parameters:

- 
grid
Specifies the grid size as a list of integers.

- 
block
Specifies the block size as a list of integers.

- 
cluster
Specifies the cluster size as a list of integers.

- 
smem
Specifies the size of shared memory in bytes (integer).

- 
None (default) — Automatically calculates the kernel’s shared memory usage via cutlass.memory.SmemAllocator. Recommended unless manual control is required.

- 
int — Manually specifies the size of shared memory in bytes.

Additional Kernel Launch Parameters:

- 
fallback_cluster
Specifies the minimum-guaranteed cluster size. When set, cluster becomes the preferred size, enabling graceful degradation when hardware cannot satisfy the preferred dimensions.

- 
None (default) — No fallback; cluster is used directly.

- 
list[int] — Three-element list [x, y, z].

- 
max_number_threads
Specifies the maximum thread count per block (maxntid).

- 
[0, 0, 0] (default) — Auto-generate reqntid from block.

- 
list[int] — Three-element list [x, y, z].

- 
min_blocks_per_mp
Specifies the minimum blocks per multiprocessor (minctasm).

- 
0 (default) — No minimum occupancy hint.

- 
int — Minimum number of blocks per multiprocessor.

- 
use_pdl
Enables Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL) to overlap dependent kernel launches in the same stream.

- 
False (default) — PDL disabled.

- 
True — PDL enabled.

- 
cooperative
Enables cooperative kernel launch; all thread blocks launch cooperatively with grid-wide synchronization support.

- 
False (default) — Standard kernel launch.

- 
True — Cooperative kernel launch.

- 
smem_merge_branch_allocs
Enables mutually exclusive control flow branches (sequentially executed if-else) to reuse the same shared memory.

- 
False (default) — Shared memory is allocated additively across all branches (default CUDA C++ behavior).

- 
True — Merge shared-memory allocations across branches (experimental feature, recommended for mega-kernels).

- 
preferred_smem_carveout
Set per-kernel hint specifying what percentage of SM on-chip memory to reserve for shared memory vs. L1 cache.

- 
None (default) — Auto calculate the percentage using formula ceil_div(min_blocks_per_mp * smem * 100, max_smem_per_mp) when min_blocks_per_mp is greater than 1

- 
int — Override the auto-calculated percentage and manually set hint.

- 
hint_smem_base_uniform
(Experimental feature) Set per-kernel hint for compiler to keep the dynamic-SMEM base ptr in a warp-uniform register.

- 
True (default) — Hint compiler to keep the dynamic-SMEM base ptr in a warp-uniform register.

- 
False — No hint for the dynamic-SMEM base ptr in kernel launch.

########## dsa_kpool.md ##########
# dsa_kpool — GLM-5.3 DSA kpool-cache compress/write (gfx942 / MI300A, SM80 / A100)

The two **kpool-cache** kernels of GLM-5.3-Flash's `DeepseekSparseAttn`
layer, the path that runs on *every* forward when `index_kpool > 1`: a
`kpool-1` live tail of recent tokens is appended to the fixed `index_topk`
columns and held in a persistent cache, which is **compressed** (one pool →
one rotated mean key) and **written** back on each forward. This is the
kpool-cache path PR #52 did *not* touch (PR #52 landed `dsa_sparse_fwd`, the
attention **forward**; the compress/write kernels are a *separate* set of
Triton kernels in `kpool_fp8_index.py`). The canonical shape/contract table
lives in `src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa_kpool.hpp`; this page only restates it.

On **A100 / SM80** the cache is hardcoded `torch.float8_e4m3fn` → `tl.float8e4nv`,
and SM80 Triton cannot even declare `*fp8e4nv` in a kernel signature, so the
JIT fails on the first forward (before MoE is ever reached). This issue ports
the two FP8 Triton kernels to native vkernels with **bf16 storage + fp32
accumulation and no `fp8e4nv` in any kernel signature** — the same
two-implementation model (`dsa.{hpp,cpp,hip}`) and `gemm_bf16` storage
convention PR #52 established. The two Triton kernels replaced are

- `kpool_fp8_index.py::_kpool_assemble_softmax_rotate_write_cache_kernel`
  (prefill / short-context) → `dsa_kpool_assemble`
- `kpool_fp8_index.py::_kpool_decode_update_and_maybe_write_cache_kernel`
  (decode; first arg `buf_fp8_ptr`) → `dsa_kpool_decode_update`

(`scatter_kpool_tail_updates` / `_scatter_kpool_tail_updates_kernel` is
index-only and is **not** affected.)


########## dsa.md ##########
# dsa — DeepseekSparseAttn sparse-MLA forward (gfx942 / MI300A)

The sparse multi-head-latent-attention forward of GLM-5.3-Flash /
DeepSeek-V3 (issue #51). An external *indexer* has already picked, per query
token, the top-`topk` most relevant KV tiles (`indices`); this kernel scores
each query against exactly those selected keys and produces the combined
attention output. It replaces the tilelang
`sparse_mla_fwd_decode_partial` (+`_combine`) decode kernels and the
`_v1`/`_v2` prefill kernels, which GPU-fault on gfx942 (the decode JIT fault
is the blocker this issue asks vkernels to close with gfx942 HIP kernels).
The shape tilelang *cannot even compile* — GLM-5.3-Flash
(`qk_rope_head_dim = 0` → `tail_dim = 0`) — is a first-class, hand-checked
case: when `tail_dim == 0` the rope-tail dot is skipped at runtime, so there
is no zero-size GEMM to lower.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.hpp`
- **C ABI**: `vk_dsa_config`, `vk_dsa_sparse_fwd` (host),
  `vk_hip_dsa_sparse_fwd` (device) in `src/c/vkernels/capi/`
- **Tests (host)**: `tests/kernels/attn/test_dsa.cpp` (10 cases, incl. a
  hand-checked `tail_dim == 0` GLM-5.3-Flash case and a `tail_dim > 0`
  DeepSeek-V3 case, plus a randomized matches-reference sweep over both
  shape families)
- **Tests (HIP)**: `meta/benchmarks/test_dsa_correct.hip` (device kernel vs
  `dsa_sparse_fwd_cpu`, bf16-tolerant, run on gfx942)
- **Benchmark**: `meta/benchmarks/bench_dsa.hip` (+ `bench_dsa.sh` driver)

# Element-wise Kernels

Three embarrassingly-parallel pointwise operations: `add`, `scale`, and
`relu`. They share the same execution model — one thread per element, a 1-D
grid mapped linearly over the input — so they differ only in the arithmetic
each thread performs.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/elementwise.cpp`
- **Source (CUDA)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/elementwise.cu`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/elementwise.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/elementwise/test_elementwise.cpp`
- **Python**: `vkernels.kernels.add / scale / relu`
- **Rust**: `vkernels::kernels::add / scale / relu`

---

## `add` — element-wise vector addition

### Computation

```
out[i] = a[i] + b[i]    for i ∈ [0, n)
```

All operands are `float32`.

# gemm_bf16 — Tiled bf16 MFMA GEMM (gfx942 / MI300A)

A tiled bf16 dense matrix multiply built on the AMD K16 bf16 MFMA
(`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_f32_16x16x16bf16_1k`) for the **Kimi-K3 projection
shapes** (issue #29). Today these shapes fall back to AITER's untuned
"torch solution:0" because `bf16_tuned_gemm.csv` has no gfx942 entries;
this kernel provides a real, validated HIP path so the fallback is no
longer the only option.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/gemm/test_gemm_bf16.cpp` (host),
  `meta/benchmarks/test_gemm_bf16_correct.hip` (device vs CPU)
- **Benchmarks**: `meta/benchmarks/bench_gemm_bf16.hip` (latency, TFLOP/s,
  effective GB/s, and a per-shape tile autotuner)
- **Performance**: `docs/performance/gemm-bf16/gfx942.md`

---

## Computation

```
C[i][j] = α · Σₖ A[i][k] · B[k][j]  +  β · C[i][j]

for i ∈ [0, M),  j ∈ [0, N),  k ∈ [0, K)
```


########## gemm.md ##########
# GEMM — Tiled SGEMM (Single-Precision General Matrix Multiply)

A textbook tiled SGEMM: `C = α · A @ B + β · C`, all `float32`, row-major
layout. This is the baseline dense matrix multiply — simple, readable, and
bit-identical between CPU and GPU — that later optimized variants (TMA,
warp-specialized, Tensor Core) will be measured against.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm.cpp`
- **Source (CUDA)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm.cu`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/gemm/test_gemm.cpp`
- **Python**: `vkernels.kernels.gemm(A, B, alpha=1.0, beta=0.0)`
- **Rust**: `vkernels::kernels::gemm(M, N, K, alpha, A, B, beta, C)`

---

## Computation

```
C[i][j] = α · Σₖ A[i][k] · B[k][j]  +  β · C[i][j]

for i ∈ [0, M),  j ∈ [0, N),  k ∈ [0, K)
```

All matrices are row-major `float32`. Dimensions:

| Matrix | Shape | Size (elements) |
|---|---|---|

########## kda.md ##########
# kda — Kimi Delta Attention (gated delta-rule layer, gfx942 / MI300A)

The delta-rule hybrid-attention layer of Kimi-K3 (issue #21). KDA is a
**gated delta-rule linear attention**: a per-head state matrix `S_t`
(`head_dim × head_dim`) is updated each token by a *delta correction*
`β_t (v_t − S_{t−1} k_t) k_tᵀ` and decayed by a forget gate `g_t`, and the
output is `o_t = S_t q_t`. On gfx942 today the AITER / Triton chunked
kernels GPU-fault (job 586165), so K3 serving sets `K3_DISABLE_KDA=1`.
vkernels re-implements the seven faulting kernels as portable host
references + HIP kernels so the KDA path is correct on MI300A **without**
that flag.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/kda.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/kda.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/kda.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/attn/test_kda.cpp` (host, 12 cases incl. a
  chunked-vs-naive cross-check at K3 head shapes)

---

## Per-token oracle

The math every kernel parallelises (verified by hand, the host oracle):

```
S_0 = 0
for t = 0 .. S-1:
    a_t = S_{t-1} · k_t                       # prediction from prior state

########## mhc.md ##########
# mhc — Multi-head hybrid-attention pre/post (gfx942 / MI300A)

Two of the tilelang MHC kernels from
`sglang/kernels/ops/layernorm/mhc.py` — the split-k
`mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum` stage-0 kernel and the `mhc_post` combine — GPU-fault /
JIT-abort on gfx942 (MI300A, issue #51, part 2). `mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum`
aborts JIT `init()` with *Requested dynamic shared memory 98304 exceeds
device limit 65536* because tilelang's HIP codegen never calls
`hipFuncSetAttribute` to opt in to the larger dynamic-shared cap (a per-stage
double-buffer pushes a 256-wide hidden block past MI300A's 64 KB *non-optin*
shared cap). The sglang-side workaround is to patch the kernel's
`hidden_block 256 -> 128`.

vkernels re-implements these two kernels as portable host references + HIP
kernels that run on gfx942 **without** that workaround: the HIP kernels use
*static* shared memory sized to fit MI300A's non-optin cap (no pipelined
double-buffer, no dynamic-shared request, no `hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in).

The complex fused kernels (`mhc_pre_big_fuse` — RMSNorm + mix extraction +
Sinkhorn normalisation, and `mhc_fused_post_pre_fma`) remain on the
tilelang path; issue #51 accepts either this vkernels HIP MHC path **or** an
upstream tilelang `hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in for them.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mhc.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mhc.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mhc.hpp`
- **C ABI**: `vk_mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum`, `vk_mhc_post` (host),
  `vk_hip_mhc_pre_gemm_sqrsum`, `vk_hip_mhc_post` (device) in

########## mla.md ##########
# mla — Multi-head Latent Attention forward (gfx942 / MI300A)

The latent-attention path of Kimi-K3 (issue #21). MLA compresses the KV
cache into a low-rank latent (`k_c`/`v_c`, both `kv_lora_rank`) and a
decoupled RoPE part (`k_pe`, `qk_rope_head_dim`), then attends with a
per-head query that carries its own rope slice. This matches vLLM's
TRITON_MLA / AITER semantics so a K3 forward served on gfx942 no longer
needs a vendor-specific fallback.

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mla.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mla.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/mla.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/attn/test_mla.cpp` (host, 6 cases incl. a
  K3-shaped cross-check against an independent reference)

---

## Computation

For each query row `i` (global index `q_start + i`) and key `j`
(global index `kv_start + j`), with a **causal** mask `kv_start + j <= q_start + i`:

```
score[i][j] = scale · ( q_nope[i] · k_c[j]  +  q_rope[i] · k_pe[j] )

out[i]      = Σ_j  softmax_causal(score)[i][j] · v_c[j]
```


########## moe_aux.md ##########
# MXFP4 MoE Aux — Quantization, Sort & Routed Scatter-Reduce

The five orchestration ops from issue #22 that bracket a grouped MXFP4
GEMM on gfx942. On gfx950 these are provided by AITER's
`module_moe_mxfp4_aux` (JIT kernels whose ~82 KB LDS requirement exceeds
the 64 KB limit of gfx942 / MI300A). vkernels re-implements them as
portable host references plus HIP kernels so a self-contained W4A4 MoE
serving path can be assembled on gfx942.

The five ops are the small data-movement primitives that turn a routed
MoE layer into something a grouped GEMM can consume. They are **not** the
GEMM itself — that is [`fused_moe_mxfp4`](moe_fused.md).

- **Source (CPU)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_aux.cpp`
- **Source (HIP)**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_aux.hip`
- **Header**: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/moe_aux.hpp`
- **Tests**: `tests/kernels/moe/test_moe_aux.cpp` (host),
  `tests/python/test_kernels.py::MoeAuxTest` (compiled vs fallback, K3 pipeline)

---
```

# MoE Distributed — TP / EP / PP orchestration for the fused MXFP4 MoE

Closes the single-device gap of the fused kernel (`fused_moe_mxfp4` /

# Quick Start Guide#
## Compatibility Requirements#
The CUTLASS DSL 4.4 release currently supports Linux and Python 3.10 - 3.14 only.
Only Linux x86_64 and aarch64 are supported. Additional platform support will be added in future releases.
CUTLASS DSL supports the same NVIDIA driver version as the corresponding CUDA Toolkit
(CUDA Toolkit 12.9 or CUDA Toolkit 13.3). Specifically, for 12.9, the driver version must be 575.51.03 or later.
## Installation#
To ensure compatibility with the examples and code on GitHub,
use the setup.sh file from the corresponding commit in the repository.
```
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass.git
# For CUDA Toolkit 12.9:
./cutlass/python/CuTeDSL/setup.sh --cu12
# For CUDA Toolkit 13.3:
./cutlass/python/CuTeDSL/setup.sh --cu13
```
If you just want to try out the last known stable release of the CUTLASS DSL (may not be compatible with the latest examples and code), run:
```
# For CUDA Toolkit 12.9:
pip install nvidia-cutlass-dsl
# For CUDA Toolkit 13.3:
pip install "nvidia-cutlass-dsl[cu13]"
```
The nvidia-cutlass-dsl wheel includes everything needed to generate GPU kernels.
To install a preview release, install from pypi.nvidia.com:

# End-to-End Code Generation#
## 1. Hybrid DSL: Python Metaprogramming, Structured GPU Code#
CuTe DSL is a hybrid DSL that combines two compilation techniques: AST rewrite
and tracing.  This combination gives you the best of both worlds:
- 
Program structure is preserved — control flow (loops, branches) is
captured via AST rewrite, compiling to proper structured code instead of
flattened traces.
- 
Python stays Python — arithmetic and tensor operations are captured via
tracing, so dynamic shapes, metaprogramming, and Python’s rich expression
language work naturally.
To understand why this matters, let’s look at each technique.
### 1.1 AST Rewrite#
The function’s abstract-syntax tree is analysed before execution.
Python control-flow (for/while, if/else) and built-ins are converted to structured intermediate representation (IR)
constructs.  Computation inside each region is left untouched at this stage.
Advantages
- 
Sees the entire program, so every branch and loop is preserved.
- 
Keeps loop structure intact for optimization such as tiling, vectorisation
or GPU thread mapping.
Disadvantages
- 
Requires a well-defined Python subset that the rewriter understands.
### 1.2 Tracing#
The decorated function is executed once with proxy arguments; overloaded
operators record every tensor operation that actually runs and produce a flat
trace that is lowered to intermediate representation (IR).
Advantages
- 
Near-zero compile latency, ideal for straight-line arithmetic.
- 
No need to parse Python source, so it supports many dynamic Python
features, and Python has many features.
Disadvantages
- 
Untaken branches vanish, so the generated kernel may be wrong for other
inputs.
- 
Loops are flattened to the iteration count observed during tracing.
- 
Data-dependent control-flow freezes to a single execution path.
### 1.3 The Hybrid Solution#
As shown above, neither technique alone is sufficient—but together they
complement each other perfectly.
Why this works: GPU kernels are simple at runtime
High-performance GPU kernels are structurally simple at runtime: they avoid
deep call hierarchies, complex branching, and dynamic dispatch.  However,
authoring such kernels benefits greatly from Python’s abstractions—classes,
metaprogramming, and polymorphic patterns improve readability and
maintainability.
The hybrid approach resolves this tension by evaluating Python abstractions at
compile time while emitting simple, optimized code for runtime execution.
How |DSL| divides the work:
- 
AST rewrite handles structure — loops (for, while) and branches
(if/else) are converted to structured intermediate representation (IR) before execution.
This solves tracing’s control-flow problem.
- 
Tracing handles arithmetic — inside each structured region, the tracer
records tensor operations exactly as they execute.  No need to model Python’s
complex semantics—just run Python and record what happens.  This solves AST
rewriting’s complexity problem.
The result:
- 
Loops compile to real loops, not unrolled traces.
- 
All branches are preserved, even if not taken during tracing.
- 
Dynamic shapes, metaprogramming, and Python idioms work naturally.
- 
The rewriter only needs to understand control flow, not all of Python.
## 2. CuTe DSL Compilation Flow: Meta-Stage to Object-Stage#
CuTe DSL bridges Python and GPU hardware through a three-stage pipeline.
Figure 1 The CuTe DSL compilation pipeline: Python source flows through AST preprocessing
and interpreter-driven tracing to produce intermediate representation (IR), which is then lowered and
compiled to device code.#
Stage 1: Pre-Staging (Python AST)
Before any code executes, the AST preprocessor rewrites the decorated function.
It inserts callbacks around control-flow constructs—loops, branches, and
function boundaries—so that program structure is captured explicitly rather than
lost during execution.
Stage 2: Meta-Stage (Python Interpreter)
The rewritten function runs in the Python interpreter with proxy tensor
arguments.  As execution proceeds:
- 
Callbacks fire at control-flow boundaries, emitting structured intermediate representation (IR) (loops,
branches, etc.).
- 
Tensor operations are traced: each operator invocation records the
corresponding operation.
- 
Compile-time constants are partially evaluated—values known at JIT time
fold directly into the intermediate representation (IR), enabling aggressive specialization.
The result is a complete representation of the kernel, with both high-level
structure and low-level arithmetic intact.
Stage 3: Object-Stage (Compiler Backend)
The internal representation passes through a lowering pipeline:
- 
High-level operations are progressively lowered toward hardware-specific
representations.
- 
Optimization passes (tiling, vectorization, memory promotion) reshape the
code for the target architecture.
- 
The final code is translated to PTX/SASS (for NVIDIA GPUs) and assembled
into a device binary.
At runtime, the compiled kernel is loaded and launched on the accelerator.
## 3. Meta-Programming vs Runtime: Two Worlds in One Function#
A key insight for understanding CuTe DSL is that your Python code runs twice,
in two very different contexts:
- 
Meta-programming time (compilation) — Python executes to build the
kernel.  This happens on the host CPU when you call a @jit function.
- 
Runtime (execution) — The compiled kernel runs on the GPU with actual
tensor data.
This distinction determines what you can observe and when.
### print() vs cute.printf(): Meta-Stage vs Object-Stage Output#
CuTe DSL provides two ways to print values, each operating at a different stage:
- 
Python’s print() — executes during the meta-stage (compilation).
Use it to inspect what the compiler sees.
- 
cute.printf() — compiles into the kernel and executes at runtime on
the GPU.  Use it to observe actual tensor values during execution.
The following examples demonstrate how the same result variable appears
differently depending on when and how you print it.
Example 1: Dynamic variables (both a and b are runtime values)
```
@cute.jit
def add_dynamicexpr(b: cutlass.Float32):
    a = cutlass.Float32(2.0)
    result = a + b
    print("[meta-stage] result =", result)          # runs at compile time
    cute.printf("[object-stage] result = %f\n", result)  # runs on GPU
add_dynamicexpr(5.0)
```
```
$> python myprogram.py
[meta-stage] result = <Float32 proxy>
[object-stage] result = 7.000000
```
At meta-stage, result is a proxy—its value is unknown until the kernel runs.
At runtime, cute.printf() prints the actual GPU-computed value.
Example 2: Compile-time constants (both a and b are Constexpr)
```
@cute.jit
def add_constexpr(b: cutlass.Constexpr):
    a = 2.0
    result = a + b
    print("[meta-stage] result =", result)          # runs at compile time
    cute.printf("[object-stage] result = %f\n", result)  # runs on GPU
add_constexpr(5.0)
```

# vkernels — low-level CUDA kernels and communication primitives

`vkernels` is the kernel layer for [opentela](https://github.com/opentela-ai): hand-tuned
CUDA kernels and the communication primitives (collectives, overlap, topology) that sit
beside them. Everything ships with a **CPU reference implementation** so it can be unit-tested
and measured for coverage on machines **without a GPU**, and a CUDA implementation that is
compiled automatically when a CUDA toolkit is present.

## TL;DR

cutedsl can target only a small minority of our kernels, and the ones it *can* target are exactly the ones it isn't built for. The high-value kernels are AMD gfx942/MI300A HIP, which cutedsl cannot compile at all. The real opportunity is a **separate NVIDIA deployment track** for the compute shapes we currently only serve on gfx942 — not a port of existing kernels.

## The hard constraint: cutedsl is NVIDIA-only

From the official docs (`dsl_code_generation.html`, Stage 3):
> "The final code is translated to **PTX/SASS (for NVIDIA GPUs)** and assembled into a device binary."

Its MMA programming guides are warp-level MMA / warpgroup wgmma / **tcgen05** (Blackwell) — all NVIDIA. There is no HIP/AMD backend and no roadmap for one. So any kernel that only has a `.hip` path is **out of scope by construction**, regardless of how well its math maps to the DSL.

## Our kernel inventory, split by what cutedsl can reach

I counted 33 device sources. They cleanly split into two tiers (matching `docs/ORIENTATION.md`):

**Tier 1 — pedagogical/infrastructure, NVIDIA CUDA (the only cutedsl-reachable set):**
- `elementwise` (add/scale/relu), `reduce` (sum/max, two-stage), `gemm` (16×16 SGEMM), `allreduce` (ring), `p2p_gather`

**Tier 2 — production serving, AMD gfx942/MI300A HIP (cutedsl cannot touch these):**
- Attention: `dsa`, `dsa_kpool`, `dsa_topk`, `kda`, `mhc`, `mla`
- MoE: `moe`, `moe_aux`, `moe_fused`, `moe_dist`, plus `gemm_bf16`
- Comm (HIP): `rccl`, `kv_gather/scatter`, `p2p_kv_donate/restore`, `cross_node_kv`, `fabric_import`, `pipeline_boundary`

So ~25 of 33 kernels — and essentially all the ones that justify a kernel DSL (fused MXFP4 GEMM, online-softmax MLA, delta-rule linear attention) — are unreachable. They were written *because* the AMD tilelang/Triton/AITER stack faults on gfx942; moving them to a NVIDIA DSL is a category change, not a port.

## Of the reachable CUDA kernels, the honest fit

| Kernel | cutedsl fit | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `gemm` (FP32, 16×16, shared-mem tiling) | **The one plausible candidate.** CuTe layouts + wgmma would express the tile hierarchy far more cleanly than the manual `__shared__ float sA[16][16]` index arithmetic. | But it's FP32 — Tensor Cores want FP16/BF16/FP8/TF32. And it's explicitly the "textbook baseline that later optimized variants will be measured against." A cutedsl version replaces the baseline, defeating its pedagogical purpose. |
| `elementwise` (add/scale/relu) | Structurally trivial: one thread per element. | Overkill and arguably worse — no MMA, no TMA, just a parallel map. The DSL is designed for the opposite problem. |
| `reduce` (two-stage) | A reduction; cutedsl has no first-class reduction primitive over the CuTe model that beats what's here. | No value. |
| `allreduce` / `p2p_gather` | Cross-rank collectives / peer copies. | Out of scope — these are network/topology kernels, not compute kernels. |

The conclusion: **there is no existing kernel where a cutedsl port is both (a) reachable and (b) a clear win.** The only one that's mathematically interesting (`gemm`) is the deliberate baseline.

## The opportunity that *does* exist

The dsa_kpool doc (`docs/kernels/dsa_kpool.md`) and KB note `dsa-kpool-cache` already describe a **broken A100/SM80 path** for the sparse-attention kpool kernels — i.e., the org already wants these shapes on NVIDIA, not just AMD. cutedsl is genuinely well-suited to *that* class of problem:

- **Fused MXFP4 MoE GEMM** (`moe_fused`) → the cutedsl MMA programming guides + per-tile quantization are almost a textbook match.
- **MLA / sparse-attention forward** (`mla`, `dsa`) → online softmax across two MMAs, exactly what the warpgroup-MMA + tcgen05 guides build toward.

So the strategic framing isn't "port our kernels to cutedsl" — it's **add an NVIDIA deployment track for the compute shapes we currently only serve on gfx942**, as `.cute.py` kernels gated behind a new backend flag (mirroring the existing CPU-oracle + device-kernel two-implementation model). That keeps the HIP kernels as the MI300A path and gives SM100/SM120 targets a real option where today there's none.

## Recommended next steps (if you want to pursue this)

1. **Pick one shape** to validate the DSL workflow end-to-end before committing: the fused MXFP4 grouped GEMM (`moe_fused`) is the highest-value proof, but `gemm` is the lowest-risk (tiny, already has an oracle + tests).
2. Wire a `VKERNELS_BUILD_CUTEDSL` gate and a `cutedsl/` source tree alongside `src/c/`, reusing the existing CPU reference as the correctness oracle (same contract headers, e.g. `gemm.hpp`).
3. Decide the target: it only makes sense if there's a concrete NVIDIA deployment (SM80/A100 fallback per the kpool issue, or SM100/SM120). On a gfx942-only box like this one, a cutedsl kernel can't even be run.

I'll persist this as a KB note since it's a decision-relevant architectural finding.

## Method

- **Algorithmic bytes** (the minimum the answer requires): `A` read once,
  `B` read once across all M-tiles, `C` written once →
  `(M·K + K·N + M·N) × 2` B.
- **Actual bytes** (this kernel, no cross-tile reuse): each block reloads
  its own `sB`, so `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times and `A` is read
  `⌈N/BN⌉` times → `2·M·K·⌈N/BN⌉ + 2·K·N·⌈M/BM⌉ + 2·M·N` B. This is the
  same two-phase tiling as the validated `moe_fused.hip` kernels; lifting
  it is the documented next step (see Limitations).
- **Arithmetic intensity** `AI = 2·M·N·K / actual_bytes`. If
  `AI < ridge (≈245)`, the kernel is **memory-bound** and its ceiling is
  `AI × HBM_bw`; otherwise it is **compute-bound** and the ceiling is the
  `≈1307` TFLOP/s MFMA roof.

  the measured peak is **≈2400 GB/s (≈45% of the 5300 GB/s HBM roof)** for
  the warmup shapes, even at full grid saturation. The shortfall from the
  100% assumption is the two-phase tile: load and MFMA are separated by a
  `__syncthreads()`, so the HBM bus is idle during compute. This is the
  binding limitation in the warmup regime (see below).

roofline note. The kernel's index/fragment layout was validated against
the verified `mfma_k64_pf` helper of `moe_fused.hip`.

1. **`BN = 16` strictly dominates `BN = 64` at serving `M`** (1.4–2.9×,

2. **Warmup achieves only 45% of HBM** (≈2400 GB/s, not the assumed
   5300), so the naive projection was 2.2× optimistic. The shortfall is

   limitation alongside the missing cross-tile B reuse.

**Challenges.**
1. *No usable torch on the node.* The only Python install with torch was
   an aarch64 wheel on an x86_64 node; the CPU oracle (fp32 accum, single
   RNE store) is the mathematically equivalent validated reference.
2. *Two-implementation discovery constraint.* A namespace-scope config
   struct would be discovered as `kind = "struct"` and break

   `int` out-params, and the explicit-tile entry is kept out of the public
   header (forward-declared by the harnesses, same as the moe_aux pattern).

**Future work** (the `hip-gemm-tuning` ladder, in order):
1. Cross-tile B reuse via a persistent / multi-M-tile-per-block schedule
   — the single highest-leverage step (turns the large warmup shapes from
   ~6% to ~70% of the compute roof).
2. LDS double-buffer (async-copy / `buffer_alloc`) overlapping load and
   MFMA — closes the 45%→100% effective-HBM gap, but only after step 1.
3. Split-K with an fp32 combine for the tiny-M serving regime (raises the
   block count past the CU count without changing the tile).
4. Per-shape `gemm_bf16_config_for` from the on-device autotuner (recover
   the 11–15% margin on the three small-`N` shapes).

content.text:
############ A100 port doc (the established pattern) ############
# dsa-kpool — paged tail-cache pool compress/write (NVIDIA A100, sm_80)

A latency + roofline characterization of the DSA kpool-cache kernels on an
**NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB**, obtained by compiling the same HIP device sources
(`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa_kpool.{cpp,hip}`) with **nvcc as CUDA** — no ROCm
anywhere on the machine. This is a cross-architecture portability check and a
second data point for the launch-bound analysis in [gfx942.md](gfx942.md);
the kernel math, oracle and harness are identical (see that file for the
formula and contract).

## The port (HIP-on-NVIDIA)

Three small, ROCm-build-neutral changes let the `.hip` sources compile under
`nvcc -x cu` (CUDA 12.6, `sm_80`, gcc 13.3 via the CSCS `prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1`
uenv):

  * `src/c/vkernels/kernels/cuda_compat/hip/hip_runtime.h` — a ~70-line shim
    that maps the (small) HIP API surface the sources use onto the CUDA
    runtime API (`hipMalloc→cudaMalloc`, events, props, ...), neutralizes
    `__host__/__device__` for host TUs, provides the std headers the real HIP
    header transitively includes, and maps `gcnArchName→name` so the
    device-detection code keeps compiling. It `#error`s if ever picked up by
    a ROCm build.
  * `moe_device.hip` — the gfx942-only MFMA inline-asm helper is now guarded
    by `#if defined(__gfx942__)||...` (nothing in the kpool path uses it).
  * `bench_dsa_kpool.hip` — device detection is by compute capability
    (`p.major == 8 && p.minor == 0`) rather than a name substring, with a
    loud `stderr` warning (placeholder roofs) on any unrecognized device.

No changes to the kernels themselves — the kpool code uses no gfx942-specific
intrinsics. The build is the normal CMake build: on a CUDA-only node,
`CudaSupport.cmake` finds nvcc and `src/c/CMakeLists.txt` compiles the kpool
`.hip` sources as CUDA (`LANGUAGE CUDA` + the shim include dir, per-source
`VKERNELS_HAS_HIP=1`); `meta/benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt` adds the two
executables the same way. `meta/scripts/build_dsa_kpool_a100_cuda.sh` is
just the srun/uenv wrapper around `cmake` + the two binaries.

## Correctness (on the bench node)

Device-vs-host-oracle **14/14 PASS** (prefill 7, decode 7), CUDA 12.6 / sm_80.
The compressed-K output carries only the bf16-store residual
(`max_rel ≈ 3.4e-3`, tolerance 2e-2 — identical magnitude to the gfx942 run);
the in-place live-tail update is an exact bf16 copy (`max_rel = 0`). Same
harness (including both decode coverage fixes from the gfx942 campaign), so
both the compress and tail-write paths are exercised.

## Prefill latency — `dsa_kpool_assemble` (1 warp-group/pool)

| n_pools | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|--------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 6.02 | 6.02 | 0.73 | 1.5 | launch |
| 16 | 4 | 64 | 7.05 | 7.06 | 9.9 | 1.5 | launch |
| 64 | 4 | 64 | 7.06 | 7.06 | 39.7 | 1.5 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 7.32 | 7.32 | 76.5 | 1.5 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 7.97 | 7.97 | 140.5 | 1.5 | launch |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 7.05 | 7.06 | 1.20 | 1.3 | launch |
| 64 | 8 | 128 | 8.87 | 8.88 | 61.1 | 1.3 | launch |
| 256 | 8 | 128 | 9.90 | 9.90 | 219.0 | 1.3 | mem |

## Decode latency — `dsa_kpool_decode_update` (1 warp-group/request)

| batch | ps | tail | us(min) | us(med) | GB/s | AI | bound |
|------:|---:|-----:|--------:|--------:|-----:|---:|-------|
| 1 | 4 | 64 | 8.61 | 8.62 | 0.57 | 1.4 | launch |
| 32 | 4 | 64 | 9.13 | 9.14 | 17.1 | 1.4 | launch |
| 128 | 4 | 64 | 9.35 | 9.38 | 66.6 | 1.4 | launch |
| 256 | 4 | 64 | 9.85 | 9.87 | 126.5 | 1.4 | launch |
| 512 | 4 | 64 | 12.06 | 12.07 | 207.1 | 1.4 | mem |
| 1 | 8 | 128 | 11.47 | 11.48 | 0.78 | 1.3 | launch |
| 128 | 8 | 128 | 12.51 | 12.51 | 91.8 | 1.3 | launch |
| 512 | 8 | 128 | 15.65 | 15.66 | 293.5 | 1.3 | mem |

Roof: ~19.5 TFLOP/s **fp32** (CUDA-core FMA — the kernels use no tensor
units), 2039 GB/s HBM2e, ridge ~10 FLOP/B.

## A100 vs MI300A — same conclusion, different constants

| shape (decode) | A100 µs | MI300A µs | ratio |
|---------------:|--------:|----------:|------:|
| bs=1, ps=4 | 8.6 | 11.7 | 0.74 |
| bs=512, ps=4 | 12.1 | 19.6 | 0.62 |
| bs=1, ps=8/t128 | 11.5 | 13.5 | 0.85 |
| bs=512, ps=8/t128 | 15.7 | 21.5 | 0.73 |

  * **A100 is 0.6–0.85× the MI300A absolute latency at every shape** — the
    floor is lower (6.0 vs 10.7 µs prefill bs=1) and the marginal cost per
    request is ~7 ns (vs ~15 ns on MI300A).
  * **The launch-bound verdict is architecture-independent.** Arithmetic
    intensity 1.3–1.5 FLOP/B sits ~6.5× below the A100's much lower ridge
    (~10 FLOP/B) and ~180× below MI300A's (~247 FLOP/B) — but both GPUs are
    still nowhere near either roof: peak effective bandwidth 294 GB/s =
    14.5% of the A100 HBM roof (vs 214 GB/s = 4.0% on MI300A), and the
    latency stays nearly flat from 1 to 256 warp-groups (6.0 → 8.0 µs
    prefill ps=4; 8.6 → 9.9 µs decode ps=4) before the bs=512 tail.
  * **Caveat on the comparison**: the MI300A µs are upper bounds (unpinned
    idle sclk ~104 MHz, see gfx942.md caveats), while the A100 boosts clocks
    quickly during the 2000-launch bursts, so part of the gap is measurement
    environment, not silicon. The direction (both are launch-dominated
    bookkeeping ops, 6–22 µs per step, noise against a ms-scale decode
    pass) is the robust signal, and it holds on both.
  * No empty-kernel dispatch-floor control was run on A100 this time
    (MI300A's was 2.8 µs/launch); given the 6.0 µs prefill floor, a similar
    quarter-to-third share is dispatch. Future work: add the control to
    this script.

## Caveats and notes

  * **Timing methodology** is the same as gfx942: 2000-launch batched
    samples, warmup burst, implausibility retry (CUDA `hipEventElapsedTime`
    resolution is ~0.5 µs, single launches of sub-µs kernels round to 0).
  * **Clocks not pinned** (`nvidia-smi -lgc` not attempted on this cluster);
    repeat run of the whole job reproduced every row within ~1–2%
    (e.g. decode bs=512 ps=8: 15.65 vs 15.44 µs).
  * **The `hipEvent_t`/`hipStream_t` types and `<<<>>>` launches** translate
    1:1 under the shim; the only source-level touch beyond the shim/mfma
    guard was the A100 roofline row in the bench.
  * **What this run does NOT characterize**: tensor-core or fp8 paths, RCCL,
    and the MI300A-specific shared-memory/L2 behavior. It is a portability +
    launch-latency data point, not the issue-#60 serving-target benchmark
    (that remains gfx942.md).

## Reproduce

```bash

rsync -a --exclude build* ./ bristen:vkernels-60/
srun -A infra02 -N1 --gres=gpu:1 -t 20 \
  uenv run prgenv-gnu/24.11:v1 --view=default \
  -- bash meta/scripts/build_dsa_kpool_a100_cuda.sh
# (override the checkout with SRC=/path; defaults to ~/vkernels-60)
# raw log of the run above: bristen-dsa-kpool-bench-A100.log
```

`src/c/vkernels/kernels/dsa.{cpp,hip}` (issue #51) — the **first stage**
that feeds `dsa_sparse_fwd`: each query scores its paged KV tiles and the
integrator's top-k then selects the blocks to attend over.

$$\text{out}[b, t] = k\_scale[\,page[b,i],\,j\,] \cdot \sum_h \Big(\max\!\big(0,\, \textstyle\sum_d Q[b,h,d]\,K[page[b,i],j,d]\big) \cdot gate[b,h]\Big)$$

where `t = i*block + j`, `t < seq_lens[b]` (else left unwritten). The
host reference (`dsa_topk_logits_cpu`) is fp32 end-to-end. The device has
**two variants**, dispatched by `dsa_topk_logits_fits_lds` /
`dsa_topk_logits_fits_lds_fp8q` against gfx942's 64 KB non-optin dynamic-LDS
cap (whose opt-in ceiling EQUALS the non-optin cap — there is NO
`hipFuncSetAttribute` opt-in past 64 KB, verified on this node; see the KB
note `mi300a-dynamic-lds-no-optin`):

# AMD→NVIDIA kernel translation: GB10 verification + port fork

Investigated on 2026-09-07 whether the gfx942/MI300A HIP kernels can be translated to NVIDIA and their performance compared, using `ds5` (`ssh ds5`).

## Hardware / toolchain (verified on ds5)

- ds5 = `dgx-spark-05.inf.ethz.ch`, **NVIDIA GB10 (Grace Blackwell, aarch64, compute 12.1 → sm_121)**. **No AMD** (no `rocminfo`/`hipcc`/`/dev/kfd`). 20 cores, 119 GB RAM.
- CUDA **13.0.88** at `/usr/local/cuda` (system g++ 13.3, cmake 3.283, `make` — **no `ninja`**, so use `-G "Unix Makefiles"`). `nvcc --list-gpu-arch` lists `compute_121`; a trivial kernel compiles at `sm_121`.
- The repo was NOT on ds5; `rsync -az --exclude='build*' --exclude='.venv' --exclude='dist' ... ./ ds5:/local/home/xiayao/vkernels/` (~85 MB transferred; **gotcha: a bare `--exclude='dist'` also excludes the real source `src/c/vkernels/dist/` — re-sync that dir explicitly**).

## Build + tests on GB10: GREEN

Configured `-DVKERNELS_BUILD_CUDA=ON -DVKERNELS_BUILD_HIP=OFF -DVKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121` (Make generator, `g++` host). **Full CUDA backend builds; ctest = 47/47 pass** — including the [[dsa-kpool-cache]] HIP kernel compiled through the `cuda_compat/hip/hip_runtime.h` shim (issue #60, previously proven on A100/bristen; now confirmed on GB10/Blackwell). Interpretation: most `.hip` kernels are NOT compiled on this CUDA-only build (only `dsa_kpool.hip` is in `VKERNELS_CUDA_HIP_SOURCES`); the pass means CPU oracles + the one shim kernel + the CUDA comm kernels all work on GB10.

## The two-kernels-same-name trap (dsa_topk)

- **Issue #51** — paged-MQA gated top-k **logits**, in `dsa.{cpp,hip}`, **uses MFMA** (`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*` ×2). Harness `test_dsa_topk_correct.hip` + `bench_dsa_topk_logits.hip`. **Has `docs/performance/dsa-topk/gfx942.md` baseline.**
- **Issue #56** — pool-level radix top-k **transform**, in `dsa_topk.{cpp,hip}`, **no MFMA**. Bench `bench_dsa_topk.hip` (links only `vkernels::vkernels`); its only test `test_capi_dsa_topk.hip` links `vkernels_hip` (unavailable CUDA-only). **No gfx942 perf baseline, no standalone CUDA correctness path.**

## The structural fork

Existing `docs/performance/*/` gfx942 baselines exist for: `dsa-kpool` (✅ already ported to A100+GB10), `dsa-topk` (issue #51, MFMA), `gemm-bf16` (MFMA), `moe-fused` (MFMA). **Every not-yet-ported baseline-bearing kernel uses MFMA** (`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*`). The no-MFMA kernels (issue #56 dsa_topk, `moe`, `moe_aux`, `mla`, `mhc`, `kda`) have **no gfx942 perf baseline**. So a *meaningful NEW AMD→NVIDIA perf comparison against an existing baseline* requires an **MFMA → CUDA** port (`mma.sync` / `nvcuda::wmma`), not the cheap shim.

## Recommended first real port: gemm_bf16 (wmma)

Most self-contained compute kernel + richest baseline (`docs/performance/gemm-bf16/gfx942.md` has full roofline + per-shape tables + autotuner matrix), clear contract `C[M,N]=α·A[M,K]@B[K,N]+β·C[M,N]` bf16-in/out, fp32-accum, RNE store. A first *correct* (not optimal) CUDA path: `nvcuda::wmma` 16×16×16 bf16 (supported sm_70+ → sm_121), mirroring the existing `gemm.cu` tile structure, reusing `gemm_bf16_cpu` oracle. New files: `gemm_bf16.cu` (`cuda::gemm_bf16`), `bench_gemm_bf16.cu`, `test_gemm_bf16_correct.cu`, CMake wiring, `docs/performance/gemm-bf16/gb10.md`.

## Caveat on the comparison

GB10 (desktop Grace Blackwell, **LPDDR5X ~273 GB/s** unified memory) vs MI300A (datacenter APU, **5.3 TB/s HBM3**, 228 CU, ~1307 bf16 TFLOP/s) is an **uneven fight** — like the dsa_kpool A100.md framing, it's "how does the same algorithm map per vendor arch", not "which is faster". gemm_bf16 is memory-bound at serving M (per gfx942.md), so GB10 will look very different (LPDDR5X vs HBM3); the warmup M=8192 compute-bound regime is the more comparable row. A datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100, per [[dsa-kpool-cache]] A100 path) would be a fairer fight — ds5 is GB10 only.

## Status

GB10 foundation verified + `cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim added (ROCm-guarded, for the MFMA port). Awaiting go-ahead on the gemm_bf16 wmma port (vs the issue #51 `dsa.hip` top-k logits, also MFMA+baseline but more entangled with attention indexing).

content.text:
an explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles on an awkward
  `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape, tolerance `max_rel < 2e-2`.
- **Latency / TFLOP / GB/s benchmark + per-shape tile autotuner**
  (`bench_gemm_bf16.hip`): serving `M = {5,8,16,32,64}`, warmup `M = 8192`,
  all K3 shapes, and a `(BM, BN)` sweep at every serving `M` that
  regenerates `gemm_bf16_config_for` on device.

## Method

- **Algorithmic bytes** (the minimum the answer requires): `A` read once,
  `B` read once across all M-tiles, `C` written once →
  `(M·K + K·N + M·N) × 2` B.
- **Actual bytes** (this kernel, no cross-tile reuse): each block reloads
  its own `sB`, so `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times and `A` is read
  `⌈N/BN⌉` times → `2·M·K·⌈N/BN⌉ + 2·K·N·⌈M/BM⌉ + 2·M·N` B. This is the
  same two-phase tiling as the validated `moe_fused.hip` kernels; lifting
  it is the documented next step (see Limitations).
- **Arithmetic intensity** `AI = 2·M·N·K / actual_bytes`. If
  `AI < ridge (≈245)`, the kernel is **memory-bound** and its ceiling is
  `AI × HBM_bw`; otherwise it is **compute-bound** and the ceiling is the
  `≈1307` TFLOP/s MFMA roof.
- **Effective HBM** is reported directly from `actual_bytes / median_us`;
  the measured peak is **≈2400 GB/s (≈45% of the 5300 GB/s HBM roof)** for
  the warmup shapes, even at full grid saturation. The shortfall from the
  100% assumption is the two-phase tile: load and MFMA are separated by a
  `__syncthreads()`, so the HBM bus is idle during compute. This is the
  binding limitation in the warmup regime (see below).

## Config (default, per `gemm_bf16_config_for` — measured)

| M | BM | BN | BK | threads | grid (`⌈M/BM⌉ × ⌈N/BN⌉`) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| ≤ 64 | 16 | 16 | 64 | 64 | serving |
| > 64 | 64 | 64 | 64 | 256 | warmup |

`BK = 64` is fixed because every K3 `K` is a multiple of 64. The serving
default is `BN = 16` (not `64`): the on-device autotuner measured
`(16,16)` to beat `(16,64)` by 1.4–2.9× on **every** serving shape,
because `BN = 16` launches `⌈N/16⌉ × ⌈M/16⌉` blocks (e.g. 1572 at
`M = 64, N = 6288`) against the 228 CUs, whereas `BN = 64` launches only
`⌈N/64⌉ × ⌈M/16⌉` (396 blocks) and leaves most CUs idle. The autotuner
matrix (below) shows `(16,16)` wins 8/11 shapes; `(64,64)` is 11–15%
better on the three small-`N`/small-`K` shapes
(`896×7168`, `7168×768`, `2304×1536`) — a marginal gain left to the
production autotuner rather than a brittle host heuristic.

The explicit-tile dispatcher (`hip::gemm_bf16_with_config`) also compiles
`(16,64), (16,128), (32,64), (32,128), (64,128)` for the autotuner.

## Measured results — QKV shape (6288 × 7168), config-selected

`hip::gemm_bf16` with the table above. `actual_bytes` uses the no-reuse
model (`A` read `⌈N/BN⌉×`, `B` read `⌈M/BM⌉×`).

| M | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 5 | 346 | 1.30 | 342 | 3.8 | mem |
| 8 | 334 | 2.16 | 405 | 5.3 | mem |
| 16 | 369 | 3.91 | 490 | 8.0 | mem |
| 32 | 371 | 7.78 | 973 | 8.0 | mem |
| 64 | 376 | 15.33 | 1919 | 8.0 | mem |
| 8192 | 9697 | 76.16 | 2400 | 31.7 | mem |

The serving latency is **nearly flat** (~340–376 µs) across `M = 5…64`
because `BN = 16` keeps the grid `⌈N/16⌉`-dominated (~393 N-tiles) and
each `M`-step only doubles the bytes (A and B traffic both scale with `M`
at `BM = BN = 16`), so effective bandwidth climbs 342 → 1919 GB/s as the
blocks fill the bus. At `M = 64` the QKV projection reaches **1919 GB/s,
36% of HBM** — versus 448 GB/s (8.5%) under the old `BN = 64` default, a
**4.3× effective-bandwidth gain** from saturation alone.

## Measured results — warmup sweep (M = 8192), all shapes

`(64, 64, 256th)`. All shapes are memory-bound on the 128× B-reread
(`AI ≈ 31`, flat across the large shapes).

| N | K | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 6288 | 7168 | 9697 | 76.2 | 2400 | 31.7 | mem |
| 3584 | 7168 | 5456 | 77.1 | 2422 | 31.9 | mem |
| 896 | 7168 | 1448 | 72.7 | 2282 | 31.9 | mem |
| 2112 | 7168 | 3272 | 75.8 | 2380 | 31.9 | mem |
| 1536 | 7168 | 2452 | 73.6 | 2309 | 31.9 | mem |
| 7168 | 1536 | 2335 | 77.2 | 2464 | 31.3 | mem |
| 7168 | 768 | 1199 | 75.2 | 2448 | 30.7 | mem |
| 7168 | 3584 | 5364 | 78.5 | 2474 | 31.7 | mem |
| 2304 | 1536 | 778 | 74.6 | 2378 | 31.3 | mem |
| 3072 | 512 | 358 | 72.0 | 2391 | 30.1 | mem |
| 1536 | 128 | 53 | 60.9 | 2378 | 25.6 | mem |

Achieved TFLOP/s is **flat at ~73–78** across the large shapes (only the
smallest `(1536, 128)` drops to 61) because the kernel is
**HBM-throughput-bound at `~AI × effective_HBM`**, not MFMA-bound. The
effective HBM is **≈2400 GB/s (45% of peak)** at full grid saturation —
2.2× below the naive `100% HBM` roofline projection. The shortfall is the
two-phase tile: with no load/compute overlap the bus idles during MFMA.
Cross-tile B reuse (which drops `AI` to ≈2378 by reading `B` once) would
make the large shapes compute-bound and lift them toward the 1307 roof;
the LDS double-buffer (next rung) is what actually closes the 45%→100%
effective-HBM gap.

## Autotuner — full tile matrix (us(med), serving M = {5,8,16,32,64})

Lower is better. `best` is the winning tile for that shape.

### M = 5

| N | K | 16×16 | 16×64 | 16×128 | 32×64 | 32×128 | 64×64 | 64×128 | best |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 6288 | 7168 | 344 | 1009 | 1851 | 610 | 1078 | 445 | 733 | 16×16 |
| 3584 | 7168 | 339 | 812 | 1487 | 517 | 886 | 402 | 648 | 16×16 |
| 896 | 7168 | 338 | 538 | 1075 | 382 | 702 | 333 | 557 | 64×64 |
| 2112 | 7168 | 339 | 815 | 1794 | 517 | 1064 | 406 | 732 | 16×16 |
| 1536 | 7168 | 340 | 720 | 1473 | 480 | 885 | 387 | 634 | 16×16 |
| 7168 | 1536 | 80 | 175 | 323 | 117 | 196 | 91 | 145 | 16×16 |
| 7168 | 768 | 44 | 64 | 158 | 47 | 98 | 43 | 76 | 64×64 |
| 7168 | 3584 | 178 | 404 | 745 | 261 | 445 | 205 | 329 | 16×16 |
| 2304 | 1536 | 76 | 122 | 231 | 88 | 153 | 77 | 123 | 16×16 |
| 3072 | 512 | 24 | 46 | 79 | 34 | 53 | 31 | 45 | 16×16 |
| 1536 | 128 | 11 | 17 | 26 | 14 | 19 | 13 | 18 | 16×16 |

The pattern is stable across `M = 8, 16, 32, 64` (full matrices in the
bench output): `(16,16)` wins every shape except the three small-`N` /
small-`K` ones (`896×7168`, `7168×768`, `2304×1536`), where `(64,64)` is
11–15% faster. The default `(16,16)` is therefore within 15% of the
per-shape optimum for **every** serving shape — the autotuner in
production recovers the remaining margin on those three shapes.

## Correctness

`test_gemm_bf16_correct.hip` was run on MI300A (gfx942). **All checks
passed (0 failures):**

- All 11 K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}`: `max_abs ≤ 0.25`, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`
  (well under the `2e-2` tolerance).
- Warmup `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes `(1536, 128)` and
  `(3072, 512)`: `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`.
- Explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles `(16,16)` …
  `(64,128)` on the awkward `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape:
  `max_abs = 0`, `max_rel = 0` — bit-exact.

===== gfx942.md lines 220-end =====

The reference is `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 dot-product, single RNE bf16
store), which is the same arithmetic torch uses for a CPU bf16 matmul;
on a node without a usable torch install (the only available build was an
aarch64 wheel on an x86_64 node), the CPU oracle is the equivalent
validated reference.

## Caveats and limitations

1. **No cross-tile B reuse.** Each block reloads its own `sB` from HBM, so
   `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times. In the warmup regime (`M = 8192, BM = 64`
   → `B` read 128×) this holds `AI ≈ 31` and caps the kernel at
   `~31 × 2400 ≈ 75 TFLOP/s` (5.7% of the 1307 roof), even though the
   ideal `AI ≈ 2378` would make the shape compute-bound. A persistent
   kernel that keeps `sB` resident across consecutive M-tiles (the
   `hip-gemm-tuning` next rung) is the single highest-leverage step.
2. **45% effective HBM, not 100%.** Even at full grid saturation the
   warmup kernel achieves only ~2400 GB/s (45% of the 5300 peak). The
   two-phase tile serialises load and MFMA behind a `__syncthreads()`, so
   the bus is idle during compute. An LDS double-buffer / async-copy
   pipeline (again per the tuning ladder) overlaps them — but only after
   cross-tile B reuse, else it just hides latency on a memory-bound path.
3. **The default tile is measured, not optimal.** The seven compiled
   tiles are swept by the in-binary autotuner; `(16,16)` is within 15% of
   the per-shape optimum at every serving `M`, and `(64,64)` recovers the
   remaining margin on three small-`N` shapes. Run `gemm_bf16_bench` on
   gfx942 and feed per-shape winners back into `gemm_bf16_config_for` for
   production.
4. **Tiny kernels are below the HIP event timer** (~0.5 µs). The two
   smallest serving shapes `(3072, 512)` and `(1536, 128)` at
   `M = {5, 8, 16}` complete faster than the timer resolves, so the bench
   reports `0 µs` / `inf TFLOP/s` / `inf GB/s` for those rows (the `AI`
   column is still valid). At `M ≥ 32` and at warmup `M = 8192` all rows
   are timed reliably.

## Journal

**What was done.** Implemented the bf16 K16-MFMA dense GEMM for the
Kimi-K3 projection shapes — CPU oracle + config selector (always
compiled, 100% host line coverage), HIP MFMA kernel + explicit-tile
dispatcher (gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_HIP`), host unit tests, a HIP-vs-CPU
correctness harness over all K3 shapes and all compiled tiles, a
latency/TFLOP/GB/s benchmark with a per-shape tile autotuner, and this
roofline note. The kernel's index/fragment layout was validated against
the verified `mfma_k64_pf` helper of `moe_fused.hip`.

**On-device validation (MI300A at CSCS beverin).** Built both HIP
harnesses with ROCm 6.3 (`hipcc`, AMD clang 18) and ran them under
`srun --partition=mi300 -N1 -G1`. The correctness harness passed
completely (0 failures, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`). The benchmark measured the
serving sweep, the warmup sweep, and the full `7-tile × 11-shape × 5-M`
autotuner matrix. Two findings drove the final config:

1. **`BN = 16` strictly dominates `BN = 64` at serving `M`** (1.4–2.9×,
   every shape) because it saturates the 228 CUs. The default was changed
   from `(16, 64)` to `(16, 16)`; correctness re-run confirmed PASS.
2. **Warmup achieves only 45% of HBM** (≈2400 GB/s, not the assumed
   5300), so the naive projection was 2.2× optimistic. The shortfall is
   the two-phase tile (no load/compute overlap), documented as the binding
   limitation alongside the missing cross-tile B reuse.

**Challenges.**
1. *No usable torch on the node.* The only Python install with torch was
   an aarch64 wheel on an x86_64 node; the CPU oracle (fp32 accum, single
   RNE store) is the mathematically equivalent validated reference.
2. *Two-implementation discovery constraint.* A namespace-scope config
   struct would be discovered as `kind = "struct"` and break
   `test_kernel_kinds_and_backends`; the selector therefore returns four
   `int` out-params, and the explicit-tile entry is kept out of the public
   header (forward-declared by the harnesses, same as the moe_aux pattern).

**Future work** (the `hip-gemm-tuning` ladder, in order):
1. Cross-tile B reuse via a persistent / multi-M-tile-per-block schedule
   — the single highest-leverage step (turns the large warmup shapes from
   ~6% to ~70% of the compute roof).
2. LDS double-buffer (async-copy / `buffer_alloc`) overlapping load and
   MFMA — closes the 45%→100% effective-HBM gap, but only after step 1.
3. Split-K with an fp32 combine for the tiny-M serving regime (raises the
   block count past the CU count without changing the tile).
4. Per-shape `gemm_bf16_config_for` from the on-device autotuner (recover
   the 11–15% margin on the three small-`N` shapes).

arguments.content:
# gemm-bf16 — bf16 wmma GEMM (NVIDIA GB10, sm_121)

A roofline analysis and per-shape tuning note for the **NVIDIA CUDA port**
of the bf16 dense GEMM in `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16.{cpp,cu}`
(issue #29, originally AMD-MFMA on gfx942 — see [[gfx942]]): the Kimi-K3
projection shapes that today fall back to AITER's untuned
"torch solution:0". The CUDA kernel is the line-for-line algorithmic
twin of the HIP one (16×16×16 `mma_sync` in place of `__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*`,
same two-phase tiled loop, same bounds-checked epilogue), so the two ports
are directly comparable shape-by-shape — **same algorithm, two memory
subsystems**.

> **Measured on NVIDIA GB10 (`ds5` = `dgx-spark-05`), aarch64, compute
> 12.1 (sm_121), CUDA 13.0.88.** Peaks are *measured in-binary*, not
> datasheet arithmetic: **48 SMs, ≈252 TFLOP/s bf16** (a register-resident
> `wmma` throughput micro-kernel — the tiled GEMM itself is memory-bound
> and cannot probe the compute roof), **≈227 GB/s** (a read-only copy
> kernel), **ridge ≈1109 FLOP/byte**. The CPU reference (`gemm_bf16_cpu`,
> fp32 accumulate + single round-to-nearest-even bf16 store) is
> mathematically identical to a torch CPU bf16 matmul, so the on-device
> CUDA-vs-CPU check (max_rel ≤ 0.78%, below) satisfies the
> "matches a reference within tolerance" criterion.

## Why this port exists

`[[gfx942]]` is the only baseline the repo had. The same algorithm ported
to a consumer-class NVIDIA chip answers a question the gfx942 note poses
explicitly ("how does the same algorithm map per arch, not which is
faster"): **GB10 is a Grace-Blackwell *desktop* SoC with LPDDR memory
(~227 GB/s), whereas MI300A is a datacenter APU with HBM3 (~5300 GB/s) —
a 23× memory-bandwidth gap.** Because the tiled GEMM is HBM-bound at every
shape (`AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32`, well under either ridge), the port is dominated
by that gap and lets us see exactly where the algorithm stops scaling.

## Kernel (pseudocode)

```cpp
// C[M,N] = α·(A[M,K] @ B[K,N]) + β·C[M,N],  all bf16, fp32 accum
// Config: BM×BN output tile, BK=64 K-tile, (BM/16)·(BN/16)·32 threads.
// Grid: (⌈M/BM⌉, ⌈N/BN⌉)  — m_tile=blockIdx.x, n_tile=blockIdx.y.
//
// Each warp owns a 16×16 output fragment; lane = threadIdx.x & 31.
// A is read ⌈N/BN⌉ times, B is read ⌈M/BM⌉ times (no cross-tile reuse).

using namespace nvcuda::wmma;
fragment<matrix_a,    16,16,16,__nv_bfloat16,row_major> a;
fragment<matrix_b,    16,16,16,__nv_bfloat16,row_major> b;
fragment<accumulator, 16,16,16,float> c; fill_fragment(c, 0);
__shared__ uint16_t sA[BM][BK], sB[BK][BN];
for (int kt = 0; kt < (K+BK-1)/BK; ++kt) {
  // cooperative loads (uint2 = 4 bf16), M/N/K bounds-checked to 0
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BM*BK/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sA */ }
  for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < BK*BN/4; i += blockDim.x) { /* sB */ }
  __syncthreads();
  for (int mf = 0; mf < BK/16; ++mf) {            // 4 mma_sync per K-tile
    load_matrix_sync(a, &sA[warp_r*16][kt*BK+mf*16], BK);   // row major
    load_matrix_sync(b, &sB[kt*BK+mf*16][warp_c*16], BN);   // row major
    mma_sync(c, a, b, c);
  }
  __syncthreads();
}
// epilogue: store_matrix_sync into C with M/N bounds-check
```

Full source: `src/c/vkernels/kernels/gemm_bf16{.hpp,.cpp,.cu}`. The HIP
MFMA kernel (`gemm_bf16.hip`) is the line-for-line anchor: same two-phase
loop, same `(BM,BN)` grid, same bounds-checked epilogue, with each AMD
`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_f32_16x16x16bf16_1k` replaced by the NVIDIA
`mma_sync` on a `(16,16,16)` bf16 fragment. The correctness oracle is the
*same* `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 dot-product, single RNE bf16 store) shared
with the HIP port.

## What was implemented

- **CPU oracle + config selector** (`gemm_bf16.cpp`, always compiled, the
  *same file* as the HIP port — zero host-side duplication): `gemm_bf16_cpu`
  and `gemm_bf16_config_for(M,N,K,&bm,&bn,&bk,&threads)`.
- **CUDA wmma kernel** (`gemm_bf16.cu`, gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_CUDA`):
  `gemm_bf16_kernel<BM,BN>` with cooperative `uint2` loads, M/N/K
  bounds-checking, the 16×16×16 `mma_sync` K-loop, and a bounds-checked
  epilogue. Per-warp fp32 staging is in *dynamic* shared memory (one 16×16
  float per warp), with a **once-per-kernel** `cudaFuncSetAttribute` opt-in
  (a static guard) — needed for the 64×128 tile (24 KB static + 32 KB
  dynamic > the 48 KB default cap), harmless for the rest. `BK = 64` is
  fixed (every K3 `K` is a multiple of 64).
- **`cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim** (new): a ROCm-guarded one-line
  mapping to `<cuda_fp16.h>`, so any future `.hip` port that uses `__half`
  compiles through the existing `hip_runtime.h` shim on CUDA. (Built and
  exercised on GB10; ready for the MFMA ports — issues #51, #56, etc.)
- **Two entry points** (`gemm_bf16` shape-selected, `gemm_bf16_with_config`
  explicit-tile), mirroring the HIP API exactly.
- **CUDA-vs-CPU correctness harness** (`test_gemm_bf16_correct.cu`): all
  K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}` plus `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes,
  and an explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles on an awkward
  `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape, tolerance `max_rel < 2e-2`.
- **Latency / TFLOP / GB/s benchmark + per-shape tile autotuner**
  (`bench_gemm_bf16.cu`): serving `M = {5,8,16,32,64}`, warmup `M = 8192`,
  all K3 shapes, and a `(BM, BN)` sweep at every serving `M`. The bf16
  compute roof and the HBM roof are *both measured in-binary* (see Method).

## Method

- **Compute roof (measured):** `wmma_throughput_k` — each warp does
  100 000 register-resident 16×16×16 `mma_sync` accumulations (HBM traffic
  O(1)), so the kernel is purely compute-bound. Measured median ≈ **252
  TFLOP/s bf16**. The tiled GEMM itself is *memory-bound at every shape*
  (`AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32 ≪ 1109`), so it cannot be used to probe the compute roof
  (an earlier version that timed the GEMM on `M=8192` reported a bogus
  "peak" of 8 TFLOP/s — that was the *memory* roof, not the compute roof).
- **Memory roof (measured):** a read-only `copy_k` over 512 MiB → **≈227
  GB/s** (GB10 LPDDR, not HBM).
- **Algorithmic bytes** (minimum the answer requires): `A` once, `B` once
  across M-tiles, `C` once → `(M·K + K·N + M·N) × 2` B.
- **Actual bytes** (this kernel, no cross-tile reuse): each block reloads
  its own `sB`, so `B` is read `⌈M/BM⌉` times and `A` is read `⌈N/BN⌉`
  times → `2·M·K·⌈N/BN⌉ + 2·K·N·⌈M/BM⌉ + 2·M·N` B. **Identical to the
  HIP kernel's model** — this is what makes the cross-arch comparison fair.
- **Arithmetic intensity** `AI = 2·M·N·K / actual_bytes`. With `BN = 16`,
  `AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32` at serving `M` and `AI ≈ 31` at warmup. Since
  `AI ≪ ridge (≈1109)` on GB10 (and `AI ≪ 245` on MI300A), **every shape is
  memory-bound on both chips** — the ceiling is `AI × effective_HBM`, never
  the compute roof.

## Config (default, per `gemm_bf16_config_for` — shared with [[gfx942]])

| M | BM | BN | BK | threads | grid (`⌈M/BM⌉ × ⌈N/BN⌉`) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| ≤ 64 | 16 | 16 | 64 | 64 | serving |
| > 64 | 64 | 64 | 64 | 256 | warmup |

This is the *same* table MI300A settled on (where `(16,16)` saturates the
228 CUs). On GB10 the on-device autotuner (below) finds **(32,64)**
strictly better at `M ≥ 16` — the config is therefore **suboptimal on
GB10** and is left as the documented starting point; the autotuner
recovers the margin in production (see Limitations).

The explicit-tile dispatcher (`cuda::gemm_bf16_with_config`) also compiles
`(16,64), (16,128), (32,64), (32,128), (64,128)` for the autotuner.

## Measured results — QKV shape (6288 × 7168), config-selected

`cuda::gemm_bf16` with the table above. `actual_bytes` uses the no-reuse
model (same as [[gfx942]]).

| M | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound | vs MI300A |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 5 | 636 | 0.71 | 186 | 3.8 | mem | 1.84× slower |
| 8 | 678 | 1.06 | 200 | 5.3 | mem | 2.03× slower |
| 16 | 846 | 1.71 | 213 | 8.0 | mem | 2.29× slower |
| 32 | 1556 | 1.85 | 232 | 8.0 | mem | 4.19× slower |
| 64 | 2248 | 2.57 | 321 | 8.0 | mem | 5.98× slower |
| 8192 | 91279 | 8.09 | 255 | 31.7 | mem | 9.42× slower |

Unlike MI300A (nearly flat, ~340–376 µs across `M = 5…64`), the GB10
latency **grows with M** (636 → 2248 µs). Both use `(16,16)`, so the grid
is `(M/16) × 393` blocks in both cases — but MI300A's 228 CUs cover that
grid in ~2–7 waves while GB10's 48 SMs need 8–33 waves, so GB10 pays the
extra serialisation as M rises. Effective bandwidth climbs only 186 → 321
GB/s (the LPDDR bus saturates early at 48 SMs), versus MI300A's
342 → 1919 GB/s (the HBM3 bus is far from saturated through serving M).

## Measured results — warmup sweep (M = 8192), all shapes

`(64, 64, 256th)`. All shapes are memory-bound (`AI ≈ 31`).

| N | K | us(med) | TFLOP/s | GB/s | AI | bound | MI300A TFLOP/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 6288 | 7168 | 91279 | 8.09 | 255 | 31.7 | mem | 76.2 |
| 3584 | 7168 | 50901 | 8.27 | 260 | 31.9 | mem | 77.1 |
| 896 | 7168 | 12722 | 8.27 | 260 | 31.9 | mem | 72.7 |
| 2112 | 7168 | 30115 | 8.24 | 259 | 31.9 | mem | 75.8 |
| 1536 | 7168 | 21593 | 8.35 | 262 | 31.9 | mem | 73.6 |
| 7168 | 1536 | 17110 | 10.54 | 336 | 31.3 | mem | 77.2 |
| 7168 | 768 | 8211 | 10.98 | 358 | 30.7 | mem | 75.2 |
| 7168 | 3584 | 44007 | 9.57 | 302 | 31.7 | mem | 78.5 |
| 2304 | 1536 | 5504 | 10.53 | 336 | 31.3 | mem | 74.6 |
| 3072 | 512 | 2370 | 10.87 | 361 | 30.1 | mem | 72.0 |
| 1536 | 128 | 320 | 10.06 | 393 | 25.6 | mem | 60.9 |

GB10 is **flat at ~8–11 TFLOP/s** (only `(1536,128)` dips to 10.1) —
exactly `AI × effective_LDDR ≈ 31 × 257 ≈ 8 TFLOP/s`, i.e. it is pinned to
its **measured LPDDR roof**. MI300A is flat at ~73–78 TFLOP/s ≈
`31 × 2400`, pinned to its *effective* HBM roof (45% of its 5300 peak). So
at warmup the two chips run the **same memory-bound kernel at their
respective effective-HBM ceilings**, and the **8–9× TFLOP/s gap is the
bandwidth gap, nothing else** — the wmma units on GB10 (252 TFLOP/s) sit
~30× under-used, exactly as the MFMA units on MI300A (1307 TFLOP/s) sit
~16× under-used. The compute roof is irrelevant on both until cross-tile
B reuse (next rung) lifts `AI` past the ridge.

## Autotuner — full tile matrix (us(med), serving M = {5,8,16,32,64})

Lower is better. `best` is the winning tile for that shape. **Key GB10
finding: `(32,64)` wins ~90% of shapes** — the opposite of MI300A, where
`(16,16)` wins 8/11. The full matrices for `M = 8,16,32,64` are in
`gb10-bench.txt`.

### M = 5

| N | K | 16×16 | 16×64 | 16×128 | 32×64 | 32×128 | 64×64 | 64×128 | best |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 6288 | 7168 | 639 | 641 | 1024 | 634 | 878 | 926 | 1267 | 32×64 |
| 3584 | 7168 | 591 | 540 | 921 | 452 | 634 | 577 | 641 | 32×64 |
| 896 | 7168 | 304 | 256 | 469 | 229 | 407 | 292 | 506 | 32×64 |
| 2112 | 7168 | 570 | 500 | 916 | 363 | 627 | 383 | 580 | 32×64 |
| 1536 | 7168 | 353 | 308 | 562 | 256 | 452 | 307 | 518 | 32×64 |
| 7168 | 1536 | 90 | 87 | 136 | 105 | 145 | 174 | 230 | 16×64 |
| 7168 | 768 | 41 | 39 | 60 | 52 | 70 | 86 | 111 | 16×64 |
| 7168 | 3584 | 330 | 298 | 496 | 291 | 420 | 440 | 598 | 32×64 |
| 2304 | 1536 | 70 | 58 | 103 | 52 | 90 | 66 | 111 | 32×64 |
| 3072 | 512 | 25 | 21 | 37 | 20 | 33 | 25 | 39 | 32×64 |
| 1536 | 128 | 9 | 8 | 11 | 7 | 11 | 9 | 13 | 32×64 |

`(32,64)` wins 9/11 at `M = 5` (the two small-`N`/small-`K` shapes
`7168×1536`, `7168×768` go to `16×64`). The pattern holds at
`M = {8,16,32}` (32×64 wins ~9/11 each); at `M = 64`, `(32,64)` wins 9/11
and `(64,64)` takes the two smallest shapes (`2304×1536`, `3072×512`).
Full matrices in `gb10-bench.txt`.

The default `(16,16)` is therefore **2.3× slower than `(32,64)` on the
`M = 64, N = 6288, K = 7168` QKV shape** (2248 vs 972 µs) and 1.4–2.3×
slower across `M ≥ 16`. Regenerating `gemm_bf16_config_for` for GB10
(`(32,64)` for `M ≥ 16`, `(16,16)` only for the very small shapes) is the
single cheapest GB10 win and is the documented next step.

## Correctness

`test_gemm_bf16_correct` was run on GB10 (sm_121). **All checks passed
(0 failures)**, byte-for-byte the same harness as the HIP one:

- All 11 K3 shapes at `M = {8, 64}`: `max_abs ≤ 0.25`, `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`
  (well under the `2e-2` tolerance).
- Warmup `M = 8192` for the two smallest shapes `(1536, 128)` and
  `(3072, 512)`: `max_rel ≤ 0.78%`.
- Explicit-tile sweep over all seven compiled tiles `(16,16)` …
  `(64,128)` on the awkward `(M=16, N=100, K=128)` shape:
  `max_abs = 0`, `max_rel = 0` — bit-exact.

The reference is the *same* `gemm_bf16_cpu` (fp32 accum, single RNE bf16
store) used by the HIP port — i.e. the CUDA kernel matches the same
oracle the HIP kernel matches, at the same tolerance.

## Caveats and limitations

1. **Same algorithm, so the same memory-bound ceiling as [[gfx942]].** No
   cross-tile B reuse → `AI ≈ 2·BN ≈ 32`, which is far below *both* ridges
   (1109 GB10, 245 MI300A). The kernel is pinned to its effective-HBM
   ceiling on both chips; the wmma units (252 TFLOP/s) sit ~30× idle.
   Cross-tile B reuse (the `cuda-efficient-kernels` / `gemm-kernel-tuning`
   next rung) is the single highest-leverage step on GB10 just as on MI300A.
2. **GB10 is the wrong chip for this workload.** A desktop SoC with 227
   GB/s LPDDR is 23× below MI300A's 5300 GB/s HBM3, and this kernel is
   HBM-bound everywhere, so GB10 runs 1.8–9.4× slower across the serving
   sweep. The port's value is **arch mapping**, not throughput — a
   datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100, HBM2e/HBM3) is the fair fight and
   remains future work.
3. **The default tile is wrong for GB10.** `gemm_bf16_config_for` is
   shared with [[gfx942]] and keeps `(16,16)` (right for MI300A's 228 CUs).
   GB10's 48 SMs prefer `(32,64)`, which is 1.4–2.3× faster at `M ≥ 16`.
   Regenerating the config per-arch (or letting the on-device autotuner
   pick) recovers this; left documented here rather than hard-coding a
   GB10 branch into the shared selector.
4. **GB10/CUDA-13 `cudaEventElapsedTime` glitch.** Batches of ≳160 rapid
   re-launches (the adaptive loop's larger batches, `max_iters=500`)
   intermittently return `ms == 0` on GB10, producing `0 µs / inf
   TFLOP/s` rows. The bench caps `bench_us` at `max_iters=80` (the same
   cap the autotuner already used, where it is unaffected), which keeps
   per-launch event medians clean and reproducible (verified across 3
   runs, 0 spurious rows). A zero-drop + chrono fallback remain in
   `bench_us` as a backstop for any residual glitch.
5. **Tiny kernels are below the event timer** (~0.5 µs). The smallest
   shapes `(3072, 512)` and `(1536, 128)` at low `M` are 8–37 µs — timed
   reliably at `max_iters=80` (unlike the sub-µs regime on MI300A).

## Journal

**What was done.** Ported the bf16 K16-MFMA dense GEMM of [[gfx942]] to
NVIDIA CUDA wmma for the Kimi-K3 projection shapes — `gemm_bf16.cu`
(gated on `VKERNELS_HAS_CUDA`, reusing the shared `gemm_bf16.cpp`
oracle/selector), a CUDA-vs-CPU correctness harness (`test_gemm_bf16.cu`),
a latency/TFLOP/GB/s benchmark with a per-shape tile autotuner and
*both* roofs measured in-binary (`bench_gemm_bf16.cu`), and a
`cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim for future `.hip` ports. The whole CUDA
backend builds at `-arch=sm_121` and ctest is 47/47.

**On-device validation (ds5, GB10).** Built with CUDA 13.0.88 at
`-arch=sm_121`. Correctness harness passed completely (0 failures,
`max_rel ≤ 0.78%`, explicit-tile sweep bit-exact). The benchmark measured
the serving sweep, the warmup sweep, and the full `7-tile × 11-shape ×
5-M` autotuner matrix, then this roofline note.

**Challenges.**
1. *Bogus "compute peak".* The first roofline used the GEMM itself as the
   compute probe; it is memory-bound (`AI ≈ 32`) and reported 8 TFLOP/s —
   the *memory* roof. Replaced with a register-resident `wmma_throughput_k`
   (HBM traffic O(1)) → a real 252 TFLOP/s bf16 compute roof.
2. *`cudaEventElapsedTime` returns 0 on GB10.* Rapid re-launch batches
   (≥160) intermittently yield `ms == 0` → `inf TFLOP/s` rows, on shapes
   that ran fine standalone (confirmed: the kernel output is correct for
   all "failing" shapes). Root cause is the batch size, not the kernel:
   capping `bench_us` at `max_iters=80` (matching the unaffected
   autotuner) eliminates it; a zero-drop + chrono backstop remains.
3. *Shared-memory cap.* The 64×128 tile's static `sA/sB` (24 KB) + dynamic
   staging (32 KB) exceed the 48 KB default per-block cap; moved the
   staging to dynamic shared with a once-per-kernel
   `cudaFuncSetAttribute` opt-in (static guard), and called it once rather
   than per-launch (the per-launch call perturbed the event clock).

**Future work** (the `cuda-efficient-kernels` / `gemm-kernel-tuning`
ladder, in order):
1. Cross-tile B reuse via a persistent / multi-M-tile-per-block schedule —
   the single highest-leverage step on both GB10 and MI300A (lifts `AI`
   from ~32 toward ~2378, making the large shapes compute-bound).
2. cp.async double-buffer overlapping load and wmma — closes the
   effective-HBM gap, but only after step 1.
3. Split-K with an fp32 combine for the tiny-M serving regime (raises the
   block count past the 48 SMs without changing the tile).
4. Per-arch `gemm_bf16_config_for`: `(32,64)` for GB10 at `M ≥ 16`
   (2.3× on the QKV shape) versus `(16,16)` for MI300A.
5. A datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100) for the fair fight the
   memory-bound algorithm actually wants.

# AMD→NVIDIA kernel translation: GB10 verification + port fork

Investigated on 2026-09-07 whether the gfx942/MI300A HIP kernels can be translated to NVIDIA and their performance compared, using `ds5` (`ssh ds5`).

## Hardware / toolchain (verified on ds5)

- ds5 = `dgx-spark-05.inf.ethz.ch`, **NVIDIA GB10 (Grace Blackwell, aarch64, compute 12.1 → sm_121)**. **No AMD** (no `rocminfo`/`hipcc`/`/dev/kfd`). 20 cores, 119 GB RAM.
- CUDA **13.0.88** at `/usr/local/cuda` (system g++ 13.3, cmake 3.283, `make` — **no `ninja`**, so use `-G "Unix Makefiles"`). `nvcc --list-gpu-arch` lists `compute_121`; a trivial kernel compiles at `sm_121`.
- The repo was NOT on ds5; `rsync -az --exclude='build*' --exclude='.venv' --exclude='dist' ... ./ ds5:/local/home/xiayao/vkernels/` (~85 MB transferred; **gotcha: a bare `--exclude='dist'` also excludes the real source `src/c/vkernels/dist/` — re-sync that dir explicitly**).

## Build + tests on GB10: GREEN

Configured `-DVKERNELS_BUILD_CUDA=ON -DVKERNELS_BUILD_HIP=OFF -DVKERNELS_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121` (Make generator, `g++` host). **Full CUDA backend builds; ctest = 47/47 pass** — including the [[dsa-kpool-cache]] HIP kernel compiled through the `cuda_compat/hip/hip_runtime.h` shim (issue #60, previously proven on A100/bristen; now confirmed on GB10/Blackwell). Interpretation: most `.hip` kernels are NOT compiled on this CUDA-only build (only `dsa_kpool.hip` is in `VKERNELS_CUDA_HIP_SOURCES`); the pass means CPU oracles + the one shim kernel + the CUDA comm kernels all work on GB10.

## The two-kernels-same-name trap (dsa_topk)

- **Issue #51** — paged-MQA gated top-k **logits**, in `dsa.{cpp,hip}`, **uses MFMA** (`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*` ×2). Harness `test_dsa_topk_correct.hip` + `bench_dsa_topk_logits.hip`. **Has `docs/performance/dsa-topk/gfx942.md` baseline.**
- **Issue #56** — pool-level radix top-k **transform**, in `dsa_topk.{cpp,hip}`, **no MFMA**. Bench `bench_dsa_topk.hip` (links only `vkernels::vkernels`); its only test `test_capi_dsa_topk.hip` links `vkernels_hip` (unavailable CUDA-only). **No gfx942 perf baseline, no standalone CUDA correctness path.**

## The structural fork

Existing `docs/performance/*/` gfx942 baselines exist for: `dsa-kpool` (✅ already ported to A100+GB10), `dsa-topk` (issue #51, MFMA), `gemm-bf16` (MFMA), `moe-fused` (MFMA). **Every not-yet-ported baseline-bearing kernel uses MFMA** (`__builtin_amdgcn_mfma_*`). The no-MFMA kernels (issue #56 dsa_topk, `moe`, `moe_aux`, `mla`, `mhc`, `kda`) have **no gfx942 perf baseline**. So a *meaningful NEW AMD→NVIDIA perf comparison against an existing baseline* requires an **MFMA → CUDA** port (`mma.sync` / `nvcuda::wmma`), not the cheap shim.

## Recommended first real port: gemm_bf16 (wmma)

Most self-contained compute kernel + richest baseline (`docs/performance/gemm-bf16/gfx942.md` has full roofline + per-shape tables + autotuner matrix), clear contract `C[M,N]=α·A[M,K]@B[K,N]+β·C[M,N]` bf16-in/out, fp32-accum, RNE store. A first *correct* (not optimal) CUDA path: `nvcuda::wmma` 16×16×16 bf16 (supported sm_70+ → sm_121), mirroring the existing `gemm.cu` tile structure, reusing `gemm_bf16_cpu` oracle. New files: `gemm_bf16.cu` (`cuda::gemm_bf16`), `bench_gemm_bf16.cu`, `test_gemm_bf16_correct.cu`, CMake wiring, `docs/performance/gemm-bf16/gb10.md`.

## Caveat on the comparison

GB10 (desktop Grace Blackwell, **LPDDR5X ~273 GB/s** unified memory) vs MI300A (datacenter APU, **5.3 TB/s HBM3**, 228 CU, ~1307 bf16 TFLOP/s) is an **uneven fight** — like the dsa_kpool A100.md framing, it's "how does the same algorithm map per vendor arch", not "which is faster". gemm_bf16 is memory-bound at serving M (per gfx942.md), so GB10 will look very different (LPDDR5X vs HBM3); the warmup M=8192 compute-bound regime is the more comparable row. A datacenter NVIDIA peer (A100/H100, per [[dsa-kpool-cache]] A100 path) would be a fairer fight — ds5 is GB10 only.

## Status

GB10 foundation verified + `cuda_compat/hip/hip_fp16.h` shim added (ROCm-guarded, for the MFMA port). Awaiting go-ahead on the gemm_bf16 wmma port (vs the issue #51 `dsa.hip` top-k logits, also MFMA+baseline but more entangled with attention indexing).
